q1Solutions:
While living in the US, we paid well in excess of $15k a year for child care for the first four years of our child’s life. We didn’t have a second child in part because of the cost. The daycare was great though with hours between 6.30am and 6pm. We never left the child that long of course but to have flexibility in hours was phenomenal.
We moved to France after the child turned four. In France, school is mandatory starting the calendar year they turn 3. Our child goes Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday from 8.30am to 4.30pm. Before and After school care as well as Wednesday garderies (daycares) are available but we chose to forego this for the first year to allow the child to better acclimatize and not overwhelm them. We organized private after school and Wednesday care in English using a sitter. Next year, the child will stay after school two days a week and attend Wednesday morning care. The costs are about $60/month. We now live closer to family and have them come by during challenging times.
q3Challenges:
Having a child in May 21 implied that a lot of daycares had shut down with the onset of COVID. Finding a daycare in time for starting with work was a pure gamble, there was no choice. I took the first non-private daycare I could find (and lucked out). We were waitlisted on at least ten daycares. 
Because it was Covid, initially the day care group had to shut down every time there was a Covid case for five days. My mother stayed with us for two months during my intense teaching period to ensure that the child was taken care of. My husband was teaching on a different campus that term and couldn’t help. We continued this for the following years.
q4OneChange: In the US, affordability. In France, more integrated Wednesday care. Overall, I really liked the flexibility of our daycare in the US: no need to let them know in advance when or how long the child joined the daycare!
q5Insights:
I think my child learnt a lot from daycare: more than I thought possible. I highly recommend (a good) daycare. 
The US (or at least Oregon where we lived) had strict ratios for the care of children. So the ratios were great between teachers and children!

q1Solutions:
Over the past few years, we have lived in two countries — the US and Germany — under quite different circumstances.
In the US, we had no family nearby, so our children attended daycare from 8am to 5pm. The availability of childcare options was generally good, although there were long waitlists initially, each requiring a fee just to join. Because our family schedules changed every semester, with different teaching timetables and conference travel, temporary or part-time arrangements were impractical. We initially tried fewer daycare hours supplemented by a nanny at home, but this proved unreliable: cancellations were frequent, and good nannies were hard to find. Daycare at least offered a dependable solution, and overall we were satisfied with it.

In Germany, we have family support, so relatives can sometimes help with pickups or step in when one of us is travelling. We also have a reliable nanny. This backup matters more here because the daycare has a lower threshold for sending sick children home and turns them away more often than our previous daycare did. There is also a general trend of staffing shortages in daycare centers which means sometimes the kids cannot attend daycare. That said, we like the daycare itself - compared to many other daycares around us, this daycare has one of the lowest staff turnover, which provides consistency and continuity of care. Moreover, in Germany, daycare is nearly free.
q3Challenges:
In the US, the biggest childcare challenge was long waitlists, which left us stressed until the last moment -the semester was about to start and we still had no solution in place. There is also enormous variation between daycares in terms of philosophy and quality, so the choice of daycare really matters. Being in a small college town, our outside options were very limited.

In Germany, the variation between daycares is minimal and we really appreciate that aspect.  It removes that whole additional struggle of clawing for a spot at the "best" daycare that we experienced. People seem to judge daycares mainly by how stable the staffing is, and it is common to simply send children to the nearest one - convenient location is the key decision factor. However, reliability of care hours is a bigger challenge here, and we frequently face days without childcare at short notice.

We were reluctant to send our children to daycare for so many hours a day, but given our erratic schedules and how demanding and stressful our work can be, it seemed like the most dependable option. These challenges affected our work life mainly through unpredictability: sudden gaps in childcare meant cancelled meetings, lost research time, and rearranged teaching, and one of us always had to be on standby. In the US, the lack of backup options meant any disruption fell entirely on us; in Germany, family support and a reliable nanny absorb much of this, though coordinating these arrangements still takes ongoing effort and planning.
q4OneChange:
The main challenge for us in all of these situations has been unpredictability. I would say that emergency backup care is the most crucial change. I remember having to cancel class on several occasions because I could not arrange childcare at short notice. Maybe when regular care falls through, you can book childcare through an app or hotline and either receive a spot in a designated backup center or have a vetted in-home caregiver, with the employer covering some of the cost beyond a small copay (I think a version of this exists in some universities but I have not experienced it). 
The German system does provide paid leave for parents caring for sick children, but this assumes you stop working, which does not really work for us when we have to teach. 
More formalized pooled childcare models, for example, daycares or municipalities keeping a float of substitute caregivers on call, might also help.

q1Solutions:
We have relied on a combination of a childcare center, family support, adjusted work schedules, and occasional babysitters.

I have not been satisfied with the availability of childcare options in the United States. The problem involves not only cost, but also limited capacity, long waitlists, restricted operating hours, and a lack of reliable care outside standard business hours. Available childcare arrangements often do not align with the schedules of working professionals, particularly those who teach evening classes, travel for work, or have responsibilities that cannot easily be rescheduled.
q3Challenges:
One of our biggest challenges was the rigidity of my work schedule. My son was born during a semester in which I was teaching three course sections, with the final section ending at 6:20 p.m. Although my employer formally offered six weeks of parental leave, using the leave required me to find colleagues who were willing to cover my teaching responsibilities without additional compensation. That arrangement effectively shifted responsibility for staffing the leave from the employer to the employee.

Because asking colleagues to cover several weeks of teaching would have imposed a substantial burden on them, I was unable to use the full leave in a meaningful way. Our department chair eventually volunteered to cover two weeks of classes, and two other colleagues recorded student presentations for me. I was very grateful for their support, but the arrangement depended almost entirely on personal goodwill and still provided far less time than a family generally needs immediately after the birth of a child.

Another major challenge was the lack of affordable support during evenings and overnight hours. While my wife and I were both working and sharing childcare responsibilities, access to a qualified night nanny or postpartum doula would have been extremely helpful, particularly during the first several weeks. However, high-quality services were prohibitively expensive, and no meaningful employer or government subsidy was available.

Even after obtaining a place at a childcare center, care is not consistently available. Both my wife and I work full time and have relatively rigid work hours, especially when I am teaching. If our child becomes ill and the childcare center requires us to pick him up, we may have no practical capacity to leave work and care for him. The same problem arises when a center closes unexpectedly or reduces its hours. There is no reliable contingency arrangement for such situations, and families are generally expected to absorb the disruption immediately, regardless of their work responsibilities. Emergency backup care would be particularly valuable in these circumstances.

The lack of childcare support has also significantly limited my participation in professional conferences. Before my child was born, I regularly attended at least three conferences each year. Since his birth, I have not been able to maintain that level of participation. None of the major conferences in my field provides on-site childcare. Attending a conference therefore generally requires me to leave our child at home with my wife, who also works full time and does not have the capacity to manage childcare alone for several consecutive days. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that many professional conferences overlap with weekends, when regular childcare is typically unavailable.

As a result, childcare constraints have affected not only our daily work schedules but also my ability to participate in activities that are important for research collaboration, professional visibility, networking, and career development. The burden can be particularly significant for researchers with young children who do not have nearby family support.

These constraints created significant sleep deprivation, scheduling pressure, and uncertainty for both of us. They also made it difficult to separate work responsibilities from recovery, newborn care, and family needs. More broadly, the experience showed me that childcare availability cannot be evaluated only by whether a daytime childcare slot exists. Reliability, operating hours, backup options, support during the period immediately following birth, and childcare during work-related travel are equally important.
q4OneChange:
I would establish automatic, protected parental leave beginning when a child is born, with the employer—not the employee—responsible for arranging temporary labor coverage during the employee’s absence. Ideally, this protection would be legally mandated so that access to meaningful leave would not depend on an employee’s department, supervisor, colleagues, bargaining power, or willingness to ask others for favors.

I would also support employer- or government-funded emergency backup care. Families need a dependable option when regular childcare is unavailable because of illness, provider closures, waitlist gaps, or unexpected work obligations.
q5Insights:
One important lesson from our experience is that childcare is not simply a matter of affordability or total capacity. It is also a coordination and reliability problem. Parents must align childcare availability with work schedules, childbirth timing, provider hours, illnesses, closures, professional travel, and unpredictable changes in family needs.

Obtaining a place at a childcare center does not mean that care is consistently available. Children become ill, centers close, and providers may require pickup with little notice. For parents with rigid work schedules, these disruptions can be nearly impossible to manage. A childcare system should therefore be evaluated not only by the number of available spaces, but also by whether families have workable backup options when ordinary arrangements fail.

Current systems often place the responsibility for managing all of these disruptions on individual families. Although families with flexible jobs or nearby relatives can assemble some solutions, others may have no workable solution. A more effective system would provide not only regular childcare, but also parental leave, extended-hour options, emergency backup care, and clearer institutional responsibility when an employee temporarily cannot work because of childbirth or caregiving needs.

Professional societies should also recognize childcare as an access and inclusion issue. Major conferences could offer subsidized on-site childcare or vetted caregiver services. Without such support, researchers with young children may be unable to participate fully in conferences and other professional activities, even when those activities are central to their careers.
